title: Ethics, Evidence and Clinical Limits
subtitle: Transparent claims, informed consent and outcome accountability
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating ethics, evidence and clinical limits within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain ethics, evidence and clinical limits without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in ethics, evidence and clinical limits.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to ethics, evidence and clinical limits.

sections.explainSimply: Ethical practice explains what is known, uncertain, burdensome and alternative.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Clinicians should work within competence, protect EEG privacy, disclose costs and conflicts, use validated outcomes and avoid diagnostic or curative claims unsupported by evidence.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: CRED-nf standards support transparent experimental reporting. Clinical services should similarly document protocol, adverse events, concurrent care and meaningful outcomes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A medication review: benefit, burden, adverse effects and alternatives must remain visible throughout care.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand ethics, evidence and clinical limits to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Precision in uncertainty is a clinical skill, not a marketing weakness.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using ethics, evidence and clinical limits predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Precision in uncertainty is a clinical skill, not a marketing weakness. Evidence classification: established ethical standards; evidence varies by indication.
